checks.claim: Key: ice giants have a bigger share of water, methane and ammonia than the gas giants
checks.note: Wikipedia: Uranus and Neptune 'consist of only about 20% hydrogen and helium by mass'; Jupiter and Saturn 'more than 90% hydrogen and helium'; the rest of the ice giants is water, ammonia and methane ices. Grokipedia Ice_giant: heavy elements 70-90% of mass.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: bigger share of hydrogen and helium (it is the gas giants that have this)
Wrong choice: a thick solid crust of ice beneath the clouds (no solid surface; ices are supercritical fluid)
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'lacking well-defined solid surfaces'; water 'primarily exists as supercritical fluid'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: many more moons (the ice giants have fewer moons than Jupiter and Saturn)
checks.note: Counts as of late 2025: Jupiter 97, Saturn 274, Uranus 28-29 (a new Uranus moon found by JWST in 2025), Neptune 16. Counts change, but the gap is far too large for the choice ever to become right; no count is keyed.

checks.claim: Stem: deep inside they are thousands of degrees hot
checks.note: Grokipedia: temperatures approach 5000 K at the core-mantle boundary.

checks.claim: Context: only about a fifth hydrogen and helium; ices so called because they were frozen solid when the planets formed; hot dense fluid; no solid surface
checks.note: Wikipedia: the compounds 'were solids when they were primarily incorporated into the planets during their formation'.

checks.claim: Context: Jupiter and Saturn more than nine-tenths hydrogen and helium, far more moons
Galileo found Europa in January 1610, one of four moons of Jupiter seen through his telescope
checks.note: Grokipedia: discovered 7 January 1610 (7-8 January; Io and Europa were first resolved separately on 8 January). 'January 1610' is right either way.

checks.claim: Stem: surface is a bright crust of ice crossed by long dark cracks, with few craters
checks.note: Smooth bright water-ice crust, dark reddish-brown lineae, few craters (young surface).

checks.claim: Key: an ocean of salty liquid water beneath the ice
checks.note: NASA: most likely source of the induced field is 'a global ocean of salty water'. The stem says 'what do scientists think', which fits the ocean not yet being directly confirmed.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: liquid methane sea; thick layer of hot melted rock; solid rock right up to the ice
checks.note: Beneath the ocean lie a silicate mantle and metal core; no molten-rock layer or methane sea is proposed under the ice.

checks.claim: Context: Galileo spacecraft's magnetic-field measurements fit a buried conducting layer of salty water
checks.note: NASA: Galileo found an induced field from 'a deep layer of some electrically conductive fluid beneath the surface'.

checks.claim: Context: ocean may hold about twice as much water as all Earth's oceans
checks.note: NASA: 'more than twice the size of Earth's oceans combined'. Grokipedia gives two and three times in different places; 'about twice' matches NASA.

checks.claim: Context: Europa one of the best places to look for life; life needs liquid water
checks.note: NASA: 'one of the most promising places in our solar system' for environments that could support life.

checks.claim: Context: seas of liquid methane on Titan; melted rock from Io's volcanoes
checks.note: Titan's lakes and seas are liquid methane and ethane; Io is the most volcanically active body (Grokipedia Galilean_moons).

checks.claim: Huygens probe descended to Titan under parachutes in 2005
checks.note: Landed 14 January 2005 after a parachute descent of about 2 h 27 min.

checks.claim: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with thick air, mostly nitrogen
checks.note: NASA: 'the only moon with a thick atmosphere'; Grokipedia: about 95% nitrogen, 5% methane, about 1.5 bar.

checks.claim: Stem: clouds rain onto the ground, feeding rivers that run to lakes and seas
checks.note: NASA lists clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons.

checks.claim: Key: liquid methane and ethane
checks.note: NASA: 'lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons like methane and ethane'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: liquid water, liquid carbon dioxide, liquid ammonia
checks.note: Water is frozen bedrock at about -179 C; no surface CO2 or ammonia liquid is reported (ammonia-water is only proposed for cryovolcanism and any interior ocean).

checks.claim: Context: ground averages about -179 C; water ice as hard as rock; methane liquid
checks.note: Grokipedia: mean surface temperature about -179 C (94 K); surface water ice acts as rock.

checks.claim: Context: Titan is the only place besides Earth known to have liquid on its surface
checks.note: NASA: 'the only place besides Earth known to have liquids on its surface'.

checks.claim: Giuseppe Piazzi, astronomer in Sicily (Palermo), found Ceres on 1 January 1801 (New Year's night)
checks.note: Grokipedia and Wikipedia: 1 January 1801, Palermo Observatory, Sicily. Piazzi saw on following nights that the star-like dot moved; 'moving dot' describes the object fairly.

checks.claim: It lay in the gap between Mars and Jupiter where a popular rule of the day (Titius-Bode) said a planet should be
checks.note: Titius-Bode law (1772) predicted a planet at about 2.8 AU; Ceres lay near it. The stem does not claim Piazzi was hunting it (he was checking a catalogue star), which is right.

checks.claim: Within a few years more small bodies turned up in the same gap
checks.note: Pallas 1802 (Olbers), Juno 1804 (Harding), Vesta 1807 (Olbers).

checks.claim: Key: leftovers that never came together as a planet
checks.note: Wikipedia: most astronomers hold the main-belt asteroids are leftovers of the protoplanetary disk that never formed a planet, Jupiter's perturbations preventing it; Grokipedia Asteroid_belt: leftover planetesimals kept by Jupiter's gravity from accreting into one planet.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: pieces of a planet that broke apart (Olbers' superseded idea)
checks.note: Wikipedia: the energy needed to destroy a planet and the belt's low mass 'does not support these hypotheses'; Phaeton article: superseded by the accretion model.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: rocks blasted off Mars; moons broken away from Jupiter
checks.note: Neither is an accepted origin of the belt.

checks.claim: Context: rocky leftovers from the solar system's birth about 4.6 billion years ago; Jupiter's gravity stirred them so they never gathered into a planet
checks.note: NASA: 'rocky remnants left over from the formation of our solar system about 4.6 billion years ago'.

checks.claim: Context: Olbers proposed in 1802 that they were pieces of a shattered planet; respectable in its day, since given up
checks.note: Olbers in 1802 suggested Ceres and Pallas were fragments of a planet that had 'burst into pieces'; the idea gained backing, now superseded. Told correctly as an old idea since dropped.

checks.claim: Context: Ceres, the largest asteroid, is now called a dwarf planet
checks.note: IAU dwarf planet since 2006. Wikipedia calls Ceres the largest asteroid in the main belt; NASA's asteroid page calls Vesta the largest asteroid (treating Ceres as a dwarf planet only). Defensible; 'the largest body in the asteroid belt' would sidestep the quibble.

checks.claim: Stem: the belt holds 'hundreds of thousands' of asteroids at least a kilometre wide
checks.note: NASA: the belt 'is estimated to contain between 1.1 and 1.9 million asteroids larger than 1 kilometer'; Grokipedia Asteroid_belt: 1.1 to 1.9 million (NEOWISE 2020); Wikipedia: 700,000 to 1.7 million. 'Hundreds of thousands' understates the count by two to four times. Fix: 'holds more than a million asteroids at least a kilometre wide' (or 'about a million or more' to cover Wikipedia's lower bound).

checks.claim: Stem: Ceres, the biggest, is about 950 km across
checks.note: NASA radius 476 km (diameter about 952 km); Dawn mean diameter 939.4 km (Wikipedia), Grokipedia about 940 km. 'About 950' is within the sources' spread.

checks.claim: Key: much less than the Moon's mass
checks.note: Wikipedia: 2.39e21 kg, '3% of the mass of the Moon'; Grokipedia: about 3-4%; NASA: 'less than that of Earth's Moon'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about the same; several times; more than Earth's
checks.note: All false given 3-4% of the Moon.

checks.claim: Context: all asteroids about 3 to 4 percent of the Moon's mass
Context: Ceres alone holds about a third of that
checks.note: Sources disagree: Grokipedia Ceres page 'one-third'; Grokipedia Asteroid_belt 'about 40%' and elsewhere 'about 31%'; Wikipedia 39%; NASA Ceres facts 25%. 'About a third' sits inside the 25-40% spread and is fair; do not tighten to a single figure.

checks.claim: Context: on average nearly a million kilometres apart
checks.note: Wikipedia: average distance about 965,600 km (600,000 miles); 'mostly empty'.

checks.claim: Context: Pioneer 10 and many spacecraft since crossed the belt unharmed
checks.note: Wikipedia: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to traverse the belt (entered July 1972).

checks.claim: Context: film belts are nothing like the real one
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Contrary to popular imagery, the asteroid belt is mostly empty.'

checks.claim: Key: the Sun's heat turns its ice into gas (coma and tail)
checks.note: Grokipedia: solar heating sublimates ices in the nucleus, releasing gas and dust that form the coma; NASA: 'heats up and spews dust and gases into a giant glowing head'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: burning like a torch
checks.note: The glow is reflected sunlight (dust) and fluorescence (ions); nothing burns.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: sweeps up gas near the Sun
checks.note: The gas comes from the comet itself.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: its rock glows red-hot
checks.note: Not the cause of the coma or tail.

checks.claim: Context: comet a small lump of ice, rock and dust, a cosmic snowball
checks.note: NASA: 'cosmic snowballs of frozen gases, rock, and dust'.

checks.claim: Context: ice turns straight into gas, carries dust to make coma and tail; glow is sunlight on dust and light from gas
checks.note: Sublimation; dust reflects sunlight, ion tail fluoresces under solar UV.

checks.claim: Context: an asteroid is mostly rock and metal with little ice, so it stays a bare lump
checks.note: NASA: C-types clay and silicate rocks, S-types silicates and nickel-iron, M-types metallic. (Rare 'active asteroids' exist, but the stem's bare lump is the typical case.)

checks.claim: Stem: tail streams for millions of kilometres, pointing away from the Sun
checks.note: Dust tails 0.1-1 AU, ion tails up to about 3 AU and more; 'always oriented generally away from the Sun'.

checks.claim: Key: the push of sunlight and the solar wind
checks.note: Radiation pressure pushes the dust tail; the solar wind shapes and pushes the ion tail.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the trail left behind as it moves
checks.note: Tail direction is 'independent of the comet's orbital direction'. (The dust tail curves somewhat along the orbit, but that does not send it away from the Sun.)

checks.claim: Wrong choices: hot gas rising like smoke; outer planets' gravity
checks.note: Neither sets the tail's direction.

checks.claim: Context: sunlight pushes the dust, the solar wind (charged particles) sweeps the gas away from the Sun
Context: heading back out, the comet travels tail first
checks.note: NASA StarChild: 'as it travels away from the Sun, the tail is in front.'

checks.claim: Halley, English astronomer, found the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 had nearly the same path
checks.note: 1705 Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets: orbital elements 'nearly the same'.

checks.claim: Key: one comet that keeps coming back
checks.note: Halley concluded they were one object returning about every 76 years.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: pieces of one broken comet; three comets passing once each; fires in Earth's air
checks.note: None was Halley's conclusion; the last two were the older views he overturned.

checks.claim: Context: returning about every 76 years; predicted return in 1758
checks.note: 'predicted its return for 1758'.

checks.claim: Context: Halley died in 1742
checks.note: Grokipedia: confirmation came 'sixteen years after his death'.

checks.claim: Context: Johann Georg Palitzsch, German farmer and amateur astronomer, saw it on Christmas night 1758
checks.note: First seen 25 December 1758 (Grokipedia: night of 25-26 December, near Dresden).

checks.claim: Context: first time anything but a planet was shown to travel round the Sun
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the first time anything other than planets had been shown to orbit the Sun'.

checks.claim: Context: many thought comets passed once on straight paths; Aristotle taught they were fires high in Earth's air
checks.note: Wikipedia: many assumed comets 'must follow straight paths through the Solar System'; Aristotle held comets atmospheric. Aristotle's Meteorology (Webster tr., classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/meteorology) has comets formed when a fiery principle kindles a dry exhalation in the upper air.

checks.claim: Key: the meteor is the glowing trail across the sky
checks.note: NASA: a meteoroid entering the atmosphere at high speed and burning up; the fireball is a meteor, often called a shooting star.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the pebble drifting in space (meteoroid)
checks.note: NASA: meteoroids 'still are in space'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the stone in the field (meteorite)
checks.note: A meteorite survives the passage and reaches the ground.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the parent asteroid
Stem: a pebble knocked off an asteroid; blackened surviving piece
checks.note: Many meteoroids are asteroid chips; a surviving stone has a dark fusion crust.

checks.claim: Context: most meteoroids burn up completely, so meteorites are rare
checks.note: NASA: 'Almost all the material is vaporized in Earth's atmosphere.'

checks.claim: Context: 'A meteor shower comes when Earth passes through dust a comet has left along its path'
checks.note: Matches NASA's general wording, but told as a rule it is not always true: NASA (2012) says 'most meteor showers are caused by icy comets', while the Geminids, one of the strongest yearly showers, come from the rocky asteroid 3200 Phaethon (Wikipedia Geminids). Fix: 'Most meteor showers come when Earth passes through dust a comet has left along its path.'

checks.claim: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930; counted as ninth planet for 76 years
checks.note: 18 February 1930, Lowell Observatory; ninth planet 1930-2006, about 76 years.

checks.claim: Mike Brown's team found Eris, more massive than Pluto
checks.note: Brown, Trujillo, Rabinowitz; identified January 2005, announced July 2005; about 27% more massive than Pluto, though about 2% smaller across (the stem rightly says mass, not size).

checks.claim: 2006 IAU rules; Pluto became a dwarf planet
checks.note: Adopted 24 August 2006, Prague.

checks.claim: Key: Pluto has not cleared its path of other bodies
checks.note: Pluto meets criteria (a) and (b) but fails (c), 'cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: not massive enough to pull itself into a ball
checks.note: Pluto is nearly round through hydrostatic equilibrium.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: too far from the Sun
checks.note: No distance criterion.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: travels round Neptune
checks.note: Pluto orbits the Sun (3:2 resonance with Neptune).

checks.claim: Context: the three criteria; Pluto shares its Kuiper belt zone with many others
Context: no distance rule; Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake are dwarf planets too
checks.note: The IAU recognises five: Pluto, Eris, Ceres, Haumea, Makemake. The context's 'too' does not claim these are the only others, so it survives if more are named.

unit_notes: Ten questions checked on 2026-11-26, Grokipedia first. One error: the asteroid-belt stem says 'hundreds of thousands' of asteroids over 1 km, where NASA and Grokipedia give 1.1-1.9 million. One uncertain: the meteor context states every meteor shower comes from comet dust (the Geminids come from asteroid 3200 Phaethon); add 'Most'. Ceres's share of the belt's mass varies by source (NASA 25%, Grokipedia one-third / 31% / 40%, Wikipedia 39%); 'about a third' is fair. Moon counts (Jupiter 97, Saturn 274, Uranus 28-29, Neptune 16 as of late 2025) are not keyed and the 'far more moons' claim survives any likely change.
